title: Common Table Expressions (CTEs)
description: Write more readable queries with CTEs (WITH clause). Learn recursive CTEs for hierarchical data like org charts and parent-child relationships.

data.text: A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a named, temporary result set that you can reference within a SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or MERGE statement. Introduced with the WITH keyword, CTEs make complex queries far more readable than deeply nested subqueries.

data.title: Basic CTE structure

data.text: The CTE definition is a regular SELECT. Once defined, you reference it by name in the statement that follows — just like any other table or view.

data.title: Why CTEs beat subqueries
data.text: CTEs can reference themselves, support recursion, and are evaluated once then reused. They also make the logical flow of a query top-to-bottom and readable, especially when you need to join a complex calculation back to the main query.

data.title: CTE replacing a subquery in FROM
data.code:
WITH cte_sales (staff, sales, year) AS (
    SELECT
        first_name + ' ' + last_name,
        SUM(quantity * list_price * (1 - discount)),
        YEAR(order_date)
    FROM   sales.orders o
    INNER JOIN sales.order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    INNER JOIN sales.staffs s ON s.staff_id = o.staff_id
    GROUP BY first_name + ' ' + last_name, YEAR(order_date)
)
SELECT staff, sales
FROM   cte_sales
WHERE  year = 2018;

data.title: Chaining two CTEs together
data.code:
WITH cte_category_counts (category_id, category_name, product_count) AS (
    SELECT c.category_id,
           c.category_name,
           COUNT(p.product_id)
    FROM   production.products p
    INNER JOIN production.categories c ON c.category_id = p.category_id
    GROUP BY c.category_id, c.category_name
),
cte_category_sales (category_id, sales) AS (
    SELECT p.category_id,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.list_price * (1 - i.discount))
    FROM   sales.order_items i
    INNER JOIN production.products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
    INNER JOIN sales.orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
    WHERE  o.order_status = 4  -- completed
    GROUP BY p.category_id
)
SELECT c.category_id,
       c.category_name,
       c.product_count,
       s.sales
FROM   cte_category_counts c
INNER JOIN cte_category_sales s
    ON s.category_id = c.category_id
ORDER BY c.category_name;

data.text: A *recursive CTE* references itself to traverse hierarchical data — like an organization chart, a bill of materials, or a category tree. It has two parts separated by UNION ALL:

data.title: Recursive CTE skeleton
data.code:
WITH cte_name (col1, col2, level) AS (
    -- Anchor member: the root rows
    SELECT col1, col2, 1
    FROM   base_table
    WHERE  parent_id IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive member: references the CTE itself
    SELECT b.col1, b.col2, c.level + 1
    FROM   base_table b
    INNER JOIN cte_name c ON c.col1 = b.parent_id
    WHERE  c.level < 10  -- safety guard
)
SELECT * FROM cte_name;

data.title: Always cap the recursion level
data.text: Recursive CTEs can run infinitely if there is a cycle in the data. Always include a level counter and a WHERE level < N guard — SQL Server's default max recursion is 100, after which it raises an error.

data.caption: A recursive CTE starts with an anchor (root rows), then repeatedly joins its own output (recursive member) until no new rows appear

Root-level rows] --> Union[UNION ALL]
  Recursive[Recursive Member
Joins CTE to base table] --> Union
  Union --> Next[Feed result back into
Recursive Member]
  Next -->|New rows found?| Recursive
  Next -->|No new rows| Done[Final result set]

items: Give CTEs descriptive names — they serve as inline documentation
CTEs can only reference themselves once; they are not materialized (SQL Server inlines them)
Multiple CTEs are defined in one WITH clause, separated by commas, and only the last is the 'main' CTE
Recursive CTEs need an anchor, a recursive member, and a termination condition

data.title: CTE essentials
points: A CTE is a named, temporary result set defined with WITH and referenced once in the following statement
CTEs improve readability over nested subqueries and can be chained or referenced multiple times
Multiple CTEs can be defined in a single WITH clause, separated by commas
Recursive CTEs traverse hierarchies like org charts and bills of materials
Every recursive CTE needs a anchor base case, a recursive step, and a safety cap on recursion depth
